newsitem.title: MEXICO: Speed is big new drug threat, U.S. official says.
newsitem.headline: Speed is big new drug threat, U.S. official says.

text.p: The world faces a deadly new drug threat from the rising abuse of methamphetamines or "speed," White House anti-drug czar Gen. Barry McCaffrey said on Tuesday.

"Methamphetamines is going to be the worst drug that affects the United States and Mexico and the globe in the decade of the nineties," McCaffrey told reporters while on a three-day visit to Mexico. "We understand it will be worse than crack cocaine."

McCaffrey, President Bill Clinton's top drug policy official, said methamphetamines were being produced both in Mexico and the United States. Taken as pills, they had become the principal drug threat in areas such as Arizona, rural Iowa and southern California.
Reviewing Washington's war on drugs, which will cost $15.3 billion this year, McCaffrey claimed that it had succeeded in cutting by half the number of U.S. narcotics users over the past 15 years.
Cocaine use has fallen sharply in the United States and the drug was unlikely to be a problem much longer, he added.

"We've gone from a figure we cite of six million casual users of cocaine in 1979 down to 1.4 million," McCaffrey said. "In 15 years ... drugs in America will no longer include cocaine as a primary threat. It's on its way out. It's known as the stupid drug."
The bad news, he said, was that American children were using other drugs in ever greater numbers, with 10.8 percent of those under age 18 consuming narcotics on a regular basis, mostly marijuana.
Declaring that "the time for finger pointing" over drugs was over, McCaffrey said he wanted to work with Latin American drug-producing nations in a partnership respecting their sovereignty.

"No one is immune from addiction in their society," he said. "We watch these things spread from Peru, Bolivia, Colombia to have a dramatic impact on Brazil, on Venezuela, on beautiful Caracas and on other nations."
McCaffrey followed the normal practice of Washington officials visiting Mexico of praising President Ernesto Zedillo's government.

McCaffrey also avoided commenting on Zedillo's recent firing of Attorney General Antonio Lozano and his appointment of a tough army general to head Mexico's equivalent of the Drug Enforcement Administration, saying these were internal matters.
